title: Cross-section of option returns and volatility
authors: Amit Goyal; Alessio Saretto
anomaly: Options on stocks whose 12-month historical volatility is far above at-the-money implied volatility earn higher subsequent straddle and delta-hedged-call returns than options on stocks whose implied volatility far exceeds historical volatility.
dataset: OptionMetrics US equity options with CRSP stock data.
sample_period: Starts January 1996; end month of the published sample not verified (the August-2006 working-paper version used January 1996 - May 2005).
methodology: Monthly decile sorts on HV minus IV, with HV the standard deviation of daily returns over the prior 12 months and IV the ATM implied volatility of options with about one month to maturity; zero-cost portfolios long the top-decile and short the bottom-decile straddles or statically delta-hedged calls. Short-leg margin was modelled with a SPAN-style scenario method (as Heston et al. 2023 describe when following them).
reported_effect: Published abstract: an 'economically and statistically significant average monthly return' for the zero-cost decile spread (gross, mid-quote); the published tables could not be accessed here. The August-2006 working paper reported 15.0% per month for the long-short straddles, 5.3% per month when paying half the quoted spread (CXO summary, https://cxoadvisory.com/?p=961); a 2017 BSIC review states the decile straddle spread yields 3.9% per month after transaction costs (https://bsic.it/dislocations-historical-implied-volatility-indicators-volatility-trades/).
transaction_costs: Treated: returns recomputed paying fractions of the quoted option spread, and short-leg margin considered; in the 2006 version paying half the quoted spread cut the mean from 15.0% to 5.3% per month (secondary summaries above).
survivorship_treatment: Historical OptionMetrics/CRSP cross-section of optionable stocks at each date; explicit delisting handling not verified.
out_of_sample_evidence: Heston et al. (2023, Table 2, https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13279) find the IV-minus-HV quintile spread in one-month ATM straddles is -10.34% per month (t=-9.48) over 1996-2019 (gross, mid-quote, equal-weighted). Hu & Jacobs (2020 JFQA, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022109019000310) confirm the relation for delta-hedged returns over 1996-July 2013. Fullwood, James & Marsh (2021 JFE, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2021.04.030) report it does not carry over to FX options.
known_criticisms: Mid-quote returns from end-of-day quotes overstate achievable returns when single-name option spreads are wide (see Muravyev & Pearson 2020 on effective vs quoted spreads); the short leg ties up substantial margin; straddle returns are extremely leveraged and skewed.
replication_status: Gross effect reproduced on later data by Heston et al. (2023) and Hu & Jacobs (2020). Chen-Zimmermann's stock-return dataset only contains the related stock-level realized-minus-implied vol signal of Bali & Hovakimian 2009 (RIVolSpread, original t=2.9), not this option-return strategy (https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv).
post_publication_decay: No clean post-2009 estimate found; the 1996-2019 sample of Heston et al. still shows a large gross spread but mixes pre- and post-publication years.
relevance_notes: Directly testable with the 2019-2024 EOD chains (12-month HV needs stock closes from 2018). Expect large gross mid-quote spreads but assume quoted-spread costs unless fills are verified; earlier evidence shows costs remove most of the edge, and ~5 years of monthly rebalances gives low statistical power. Report results at mid, half-spread and full quoted spread, liquid names only.

title: Anticipating Uncertainty: Straddles around Earnings Announcements
authors: Chao Gao; Yuhang Xing; Xiaoyan Zhang
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 53(6), 2587-2617
anomaly: At-the-money straddles on individual stocks, which lose money on average, earn significantly positive returns when bought a few days before a scheduled earnings announcement, consistent with investors underestimating announcement uncertainty.
dataset: OptionMetrics end-of-day bid/ask quotes, CRSP, Compustat, I/B/E/S announcement dates; options with 10-60 days to expiry, |delta| 0.375-0.625, moneyness 0.9-1.1, option price >= $0.125, stock price >= $5, positive open interest.
methodology: Holding-period returns of delta-neutral ATM straddles over event windows [-3,-1], [-3,0], [-3,1], [-1,0], [-1,1] around the announcement day 0, computed from closing bid-ask midpoints; pooled and quarterly time-series averages under equal, volume and dollar-open-interest weights; robustness on subsamples where the actual date equals an expected date.
reported_effect: Headline 3.34% (t=6.71) for buying on day -3 and selling on day 0 (time-series, equal-weighted, mid-quote, gross); the strictly pre-announcement window [-3,-1] earns 2.62% (t=9.67) (pooled estimate 1.90%). With dollar-open-interest weights across firms [-3,0] falls to 1.10% (t=2.00) and [-3,1] to -0.67% (insignificant). Unconditional ATM straddles average -0.19% per day and -17.09% per month.
transaction_costs: Not treated: midpoint returns, and the authors state the goal is to document anticipation of uncertainty rather than a tradable strategy. The effect is larger where stock/option spreads are wider.
survivorship_treatment: Historical OptionMetrics/CRSP universe; the filter requiring valid option prices at both the start and end of the window is a mild look-ahead condition.
out_of_sample_evidence: No independent post-2013 replication found. de Silva, Smith & So (Review of Finance 2026, 2010-Feb 2021 data, https://doi.org/10.1093/rof/rfaf052) find ATM straddles over high-expected-volatility announcements underperform low-expected-volatility ones by 11% (t=19.55), which is not a direct test of the [-3,-1] trade.
known_criticisms: Midpoint returns on short-dated straddles ignore spreads that widen before announcements (de Silva et al. estimate half-spread costs alone at about 9% of investment for high-expected-volatility events). Sensitivity to weighting shows the effect sits in small, illiquid names.
replication_status: Outside the stock-return meta-studies (HXZ, Chen-Zimmermann, JKP). Internally robust to expected-date subsamples ([-3,0] pooled 2.57% (t=10.81) and 2.58% (t=8.45) under two expected-date definitions).
post_publication_decay: Not measured. Retail option buying concentrated before earnings grew in 2010-2021 (de Silva et al.); whether this eroded the pre-announcement run-up is untested.
relevance_notes: Directly testable with 2019-2024 EOD chains plus a point-in-time earnings calendar (only dates known at entry; mind before-open vs after-close timing). Test the exit-before-announcement window [-3,-1] separately from holding through day 0/1, at mid and at quoted spreads; expect spreads to consume much of a 2-3% gross edge, especially in the small names where it is strongest.

title: Option Momentum
authors: Steven L. Heston; Christopher S. Jones; Mehdi Khorram; Shuaiqi Li; Haitao Mo
anomaly: Equity straddles with high average returns over the past 2-12 months (and up to 36 months) outperform straddles with low past returns over the next month, while one-month past straddle returns reverse.
dataset: OptionMetrics one-month approximately-ATM zero-delta straddles on US stocks (about 385,000 straddle-month observations, about 1,369 per month); CRSP. Author copy: http://faculty.marshall.usc.edu/Christopher-Jones/pdf/opmom.pdf
methodology: On each third Friday, straddles are sorted into equal-weighted quintiles on average past monthly straddle returns over various lag windows and held to expiration, with returns from bid-ask midpoints. Robustness with OTM options, delta-hedging, Fama-MacBeth controls, factor models, after-cost returns and margin adjustment.
reported_effect: Gross, mid-quote: lag 2-12 high-minus-low quintile 6.22% per month (t=7.97); lag-1 reversal -4.09% per month (t=-6.18); annualized Sharpe of past-year momentum 1.53 (monthly 0.441). The average straddle returns -5.3% per month with 81% monthly standard deviation.
transaction_costs: Treated (Table 13): paying the full quoted spread turns main-sample momentum into -6.78% per month (t=-9.63), 'effective' spreads (75.8% of quoted) give -3.56%, 'adjusted' (51.6%) -0.40%, and only 'algo-trader' costs (20.3%, from Muravyev-Pearson) leave +3.62% (t=4.81). Deciles restricted to options with spreads under 10% of mid keep 2.60% (t=1.75) at effective and 1.12% (t=0.75) at quoted spreads; margin adjustment cuts gross returns by 50-55%.
survivorship_treatment: Historical OptionMetrics/CRSP universe with a positive-open-interest filter; delisting handling not described in the text reviewed.
out_of_sample_evidence: Within-sample only: momentum is significant in every five-year subsample of 1996-2019 and in almost all size, liquidity, coverage and rating subgroups. No independent post-2019 test found.
known_criticisms: Profits vanish for a liquidity taker unless algorithmic-trader execution is achieved (authors' own Table 13); short-straddle legs require heavy margin; end-of-day midpoint returns may overstate achievable returns.
replication_status: Authors' robustness only; option-return predictors are outside the HXZ/Chen-Zimmermann/JKP stock-return replication sets.
post_publication_decay: Too recent (published 2023, sample ends 2019) for post-publication evidence.
relevance_notes: Testable only from about 2020 with 2019-2024 chains (needs 2-12 months of straddle history), so roughly 4-5 years of monthly observations. The authors' own cost table implies losses at quoted or effective spreads; a paper lab cannot assume algo-level fills, so evaluate at full quoted spreads and treat net profitability as doubtful.

title: Cross section of option returns and idiosyncratic stock volatility
authors: Jie Cao; Bing Han
anomaly: Delta-hedged equity option returns decrease monotonically with the underlying stock's idiosyncratic volatility, i.e. options on high-IVOL stocks are expensive.
dataset: OptionMetrics Ivy DB (closing bid/ask, volume, open interest, delta), CRSP, Compustat; about 210,000 delta-hedged option returns on about 6,000 stocks. Accepted manuscript: https://utoronto.scholaris.ca/bitstreams/9a194795-47c8-4979-b07f-3e15445d967b/download
methodology: Each month-end take the call and put closest to ATM with the shortest maturity above one month; compute delta-hedged gains with daily hedge rebalancing, scaled by the initial hedged position; Fama-MacBeth regressions and quintile/decile sorts on FF3 idiosyncratic volatility.
reported_effect: Long delta-hedged calls on the bottom-IVOL quintile and short on the top quintile earns about 1.40% per month at midpoints (equal-weighted, gross). The spread is 1.63% per month in the smallest size quintile but 0.32% in the largest, and exceeds 1% per month in each of 1996-99, 2000-03, 2004-06 and 2007-09.
transaction_costs: Treated: with effective spreads of 10% / 25% / 50% of quoted the quintile spread falls to 1.16% / 0.79% / 0.17% per month (the last insignificant); the decile version is significant at 50% but not at 75%. Authors conclude only low-cost traders can exploit it.
survivorship_treatment: Historical OptionMetrics/CRSP cross-section; excludes calls whose stock pays a dividend before expiry; delisting handling not described in text reviewed.
out_of_sample_evidence: Hu & Jacobs (2020 JFQA, 1996-July 2013, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022109019000310) report a significant negative volatility/delta-hedged-return relation for calls and puts. Heston et al. (2023) find the idiosyncratic-vol quintile spread in straddle returns is -2.49% per month (t=-1.99) over 1996-2019. Zhan, Han, Cao & Tong (2022 RFS 35(3), https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/rfinst/v35y2022i3p1394-1442..html) extend to many characteristics, reporting Sharpe ratios above two that remain profitable after costs.
known_criticisms: Concentrated in small, illiquid, low-priced stocks; the pricing pattern lies inside the no-arbitrage band for most traders; limits-to-arbitrage controls cut the relation by about 40%; daily delta-hedging adds stock-trading costs.
replication_status: Confirmed on overlapping data by Hu & Jacobs (2020) and in straddles by Heston et al. (2023); not part of stock-return replication datasets.
post_publication_decay: No direct post-2013 estimate found.
relevance_notes: Testable for 2019-2024 with EOD chains and daily stock closes for hedging. In a liquid large-cap universe expect the weak end (0.32% per month gross in the top size quintile), well below likely spread costs; only worth running as a short-vol tilt if fills near mid can be justified.

title: Equity Volatility Term Structures and the Cross Section of Option Returns
authors: Aurelio Vasquez
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 52(6), 2727-2754
anomaly: Straddles on stocks with an upward-sloping implied-volatility term structure (long-dated ATM IV above short-dated) outperform straddles on stocks with a downward-sloping term structure.
dataset: OptionMetrics ATM implied volatilities and option quotes for US stocks (working-paper version: about 260 stocks per month).
sample_period: Working-paper version (October 2011): January 1996 - June 2007; published sample end not verified.
methodology: Rank stocks monthly on the slope of the ATM implied-volatility term structure and form decile portfolios of straddles (also naked and delta-hedged calls and puts), long high-slope and short low-slope; tests against traditional factors, higher-order option factors and jump risk.
reported_effect: Published abstract: high-slope straddle portfolios outperform low-slope ones by an economically and statistically significant amount. Working paper (CXO summary, https://www.cxoadvisory.com/volatility-effects/exploiting-the-implied-volatility-term-structure/): decile straddle spread 27.1% per month gross (29.9% in 1996-2000, 24.9% in 2001-2007).
transaction_costs: Treated in the working paper: 12.3% per month net with frictions equal to the bid-ask spread and 10.9% per month at 1.1 times the spread (CXO summary); published net figures not verified.
survivorship_treatment: Historical OptionMetrics universe with liquidity filters; delisting handling not verified.
out_of_sample_evidence: Heston et al. (2023, Table 2, 1996-2019, equal-weighted one-month ATM straddles, mid-quote) find the IV term-spread high-minus-low quintile earns 7.17% per month (t=7.92), consistent with persistence through 2019.
known_criticisms: Gross returns are midpoint-based on wide-spread single-name options and highly leveraged; the short-straddle leg needs margin; no independent net-of-cost replication found.
replication_status: Gross effect reproduced as a control characteristic by Heston et al. (2023); Hu & Jacobs (2020) also cite it as an established option-return pattern.
post_publication_decay: No post-2017 evidence found (Heston et al.'s sample contains only about two post-publication years).
relevance_notes: Testable with 2019-2024 EOD chains (needs at least two expiries per name). Scheduled events inside the front expiry (earnings) invert the term structure, so control with a point-in-time event calendar to avoid confounding with the Gao-Xing-Zhang effect; evaluate at quoted spreads.

title: What Does the Individual Option Volatility Smirk Tell Us About Future Equity Returns?
authors: Yuhang Xing; Xiaoyan Zhang; Rui Zhao
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 45(3), 641-662
anomaly: Stocks whose OTM puts carry much higher implied volatility than ATM calls (steep smirk) subsequently underperform stocks with flat smirks.
dataset: OptionMetrics, CRSP, Compustat, I/B/E/S; about 840 firms per week, tilted to large, liquid optionable stocks.
methodology: SKEW = IV of the OTM put (strike/spot 0.80-0.95, closest to 0.95) minus IV of the ATM call (strike/spot 0.95-1.05, closest to 1), 10-60 days to expiry, averaged Tuesday-to-Tuesday; skip one day; weekly value-weighted quintile portfolios and Fama-MacBeth regressions.
reported_effect: Lowest-minus-highest SKEW quintile: 16 bp per week raw (9.19% per year, t=2.19) and 21 bp per week FF3 alpha (10.90% annualized, t=2.93), value-weighted, gross. Predictability persists at least 6 months; steep-smirk firms have the worst subsequent earnings surprises.
transaction_costs: Not treated (weekly rebalanced long-short stock portfolios).
survivorship_treatment: CRSP/OptionMetrics historical universe of optionable stocks; delisting treatment not stated in text reviewed.
out_of_sample_evidence: No post-2005 test reviewed. Heston et al. (2023) find the smirk slope does not predict straddle returns (quintile spread 0.49%, t=0.78), a different target than stock returns.
known_criticisms: Raw-return t-statistic only 2.19 over 10 years; weekly turnover; several closely related option-implied signals exist (e.g., Yan 2011 smile slope, Bali & Hovakimian 2009 call-put spread), so incremental value must be tested jointly.
replication_status: Chen-Zimmermann include it as 'skew1' with original evidence classed 'likely' (t=2.19) and reproduction quality 'fair' (https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv); reproduced t-stat not checked here.
post_publication_decay: No signal-specific estimate found; the McLean-Pontiff average post-publication decline (58%) is the default prior.
relevance_notes: Testable for 2019-2024: compute SKEW from EOD chains and trade the stocks (cheaper than options). Use weekly or monthly rebalancing in a liquid universe; a 21 bp/week gross alpha would be largely consumed by weekly turnover outside the most liquid names.

title: Losing is optional: retail option trading and expected announcement volatility
authors: Tim de Silva; Kevin Smith; Eric C. So
venue: Review of Finance 30(2), 489-535 (advance access 24 October 2025; SSRN 4050165)
anomaly: Retail investors buy options in a concentrated way before earnings announcements with high expected volatility, overpay relative to realized volatility, pay large spreads and close late; high-expected-volatility announcement straddles underperform.
dataset: Nasdaq NOTO/PHOTO clientele-level opening/closing volume for the Nasdaq Options Market and PHLX, OptionMetrics, CRSP, Compustat, Factiva; 32,758 quarterly earnings announcements. Author copy: https://www.timdesilva.me/files/papers/losing_optional.pdf
methodology: Relate retail option demand to expected announcement volatility (EAV); compare ATM straddle returns around announcements across EAV groups; track clientele positions in event time to estimate wealth transfers including half-spread costs.
reported_effect: ATM straddles on high-EAV announcements underperform low-EAV ones by 11% on average (t=19.55) and by a further 9% over the following two weeks (t=8.26). Retail investors lose 5-9% of option investment around announcements on average and 10-14% for high-EAV events (about $3 billion over the sample); half-spreads alone cost about 9% for high-EAV events.
transaction_costs: Explicitly included (half-spread with conservative price-improvement assumptions).
out_of_sample_evidence: Authors report qualitatively and quantitatively similar results in an earlier sample ending December 2019.
known_criticisms: Retail identification relies on order-origin codes from two exchanges; the straddle comparison across EAV groups is relative, not a standalone net-of-margin short strategy.
replication_status: No independent replication reviewed.
post_publication_decay: Too recent.
relevance_notes: Counterweight to Gao-Xing-Zhang for 2019-2024: options on high-expected-move announcements look overpriced. The EOD chains can test straddle P&L by implied-move bucket around point-in-time earnings dates, net of quoted spreads, which are large exactly where retail demand concentrates.

title: Options Trading Costs Are Lower than You Think
authors: Dmitriy Muravyev; Neil D. Pearson
anomaly: Option price changes are predictable at high frequency, so traders who time executions pay effective spreads far below conventional (quoted-spread) estimates.
dataset: Intraday option trades and quotes for 37 stocks and 2 ETFs (per CXO summary, https://www.cxoadvisory.com/equity-options/timing-option-trades-to-suppress-trading-frictions/).
sample_period: April 2003 - October 2006 (882 trading days, per CXO summary).
methodology: Estimate option fair value from high-frequency quote dynamics and measure effective spreads relative to fair value; identify trades that exploit predictable quote moves.
reported_effect: Effective spreads of traders who time executions are less than 40% of conventional measures, and the overall average effective spread is one-quarter smaller (abstract). As used by Heston et al. (2023): algo, adjusted and effective spreads equal 20.3%, 51.6% and 75.8% of quoted spreads (algo traders pay a $0.026 effective half-spread vs $0.128 quoted for ATM options).
transaction_costs: This is the cost study.
known_criticisms: Short 2003-2006 sample of liquid names; achieving these costs requires intraday fair-value models and algorithmic execution.
replication_status: Used as the cost benchmark by Heston et al. (2023).
relevance_notes: With only EOD chains the lab cannot observe intraday fair value or verify timed fills, so assume quoted or near-quoted spreads and report sensitivity at 25/50/75/100% of quoted; any edge that only survives at 'algo' costs is not demonstrable here.

title: Fads, Martingales, and Market Efficiency
authors: Bruce N. Lehmann
anomaly: Stocks that were relative winners (losers) in one week experience sizeable return reversals the following week.
dataset: CRSP daily returns for NYSE and AMEX securities, aggregated to Wednesday-Tuesday weeks. NBER WP: https://www.nber.org/papers/w2533
methodology: Costless portfolios with weights proportional to minus each security's prior-week return relative to the cross-sectional average, scaled to $1 long and $1 short; profits over subsequent weeks aggregated into 26-week periods; checks for bid-ask bounce and thin trading (four-day returns) and for one-way transaction costs.
reported_effect: The two one-week strategies earned strictly positive gross profits in every one of the 49 six-month periods (and all 98 quarterly and 24 annual observations); weekly profits of 1-4% per $1 long/$1 short were typical. Strategies based on returns two or more weeks back were much weaker.
transaction_costs: Treated: one-way costs of 0.05%-0.4% per dollar traded; the one-week strategies still showed measured arbitrage profits at 0.05%-0.2% (floor traders, large managers), ignoring price impact of more than 2,000 trades per week.
survivorship_treatment: Requires each security to be listed both in the formation week and k weeks later - a look-ahead/survivorship condition the author acknowledges, arguing that delisting over a few weeks is small enough to have a negligible effect.
out_of_sample_evidence: Khandani & Lo (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.finmar.2010.07.005) find a closely related daily contrarian strategy fell from 1.38% per day (1995) to 0.13% per day (2007) gross; de Groot, Huij & Zhou (2012) find standard reversal net-negative in a broad universe but positive among large caps with low-turnover construction.
known_criticisms: Part of measured profit reflects bid-ask bounce, nonsynchronous trading and lead-lag effects (Lo & MacKinlay 1990); costs and price impact of weekly trading of thousands of names are understated; returns may compensate liquidity provision.
replication_status: Monthly analogue reproduced by Chen-Zimmermann (Jegadeesh 1990 STreversal, original t=12.44, equal-weighted deciles; https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv). HXZ (2017 WP, https://conference.nber.org/conf_papers/f102921/f102921.pdf) find the NYSE-breakpoint value-weighted monthly reversal spread only -0.26% per month (t=-1.31).
post_publication_decay: Strong: Khandani & Lo document a near-monotonic decline 1995-2007; Medhat & Schmeling (2022) report the low-turnover reversal effect tapered off after 2011.
relevance_notes: Testable with daily data, but in liquid large caps expect gross returns of a few bp per day at most and turnover of several hundred percent per week; net profitability needs a large-cap universe, buffered (low-turnover) construction and stock-level costs as in de Groot et al.

title: When Are Contrarian Profits Due to Stock Market Overreaction?
authors: Andrew W. Lo; A. Craig MacKinlay
anomaly: Weekly contrarian profits come largely from positive cross-autocorrelations (large stocks lead small stocks) rather than from overreaction.
dataset: CRSP NYSE/AMEX daily returns compounded to weekly, plus size-sorted portfolios. NBER WP: https://www.nber.org/papers/w2977
methodology: Contrarian weights equal to minus (1/N)(own prior-week return minus equal-weighted market return); decomposition of expected profits into autocovariance, cross-autocovariance and cross-sectional variance terms; size-quintile lead-lag analysis.
reported_effect: At lag 1 about half of expected contrarian profits come from positive cross-autocovariances (about 67% in the central size quintile); the authors conclude that less than 50% of expected profits can be attributed to overreaction, and that large-stock returns lead small-stock returns.
transaction_costs: not treated
survivorship_treatment: Main analysis uses stocks continuously listed for over 20 years, which the authors acknowledge induces survivorship bias; half-sample subsets give virtually identical patterns.
out_of_sample_evidence: Khandani & Lo (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.finmar.2010.07.005) apply this strategy to 1995-2007: average daily returns fell from 1.38% (1995) to 0.13% (2007), with near-zero returns in the largest size decile throughout.
known_criticisms: Nonsynchronous trading and bid-ask effects can create cross-autocorrelation; de Groot et al. (2012) find reversal profits not larger for the 1,500 largest than for the 100 largest stocks, which argues against a nonsynchronous-trading explanation.
replication_status: Strategy used as the benchmark contrarian rule by Khandani & Lo (2007, 2011).
post_publication_decay: Large decline in gross daily returns 1995-2007 (Khandani & Lo).
relevance_notes: Mainly diagnostic for the lab: measure the own- vs cross-autocovariance decomposition on 2016-2024 liquid stocks before attributing any reversal profit to overreaction; use a skip day and point-in-time universes to avoid bid-ask bounce and survivorship artifacts.

title: Another look at trading costs and short-term reversal profits
authors: Wilma de Groot; Joop Huij; Weili Zhou
anomaly: Weekly short-term reversal remains profitable net of trading costs among large-cap stocks when turnover is controlled.
dataset: 1,500 largest US stocks (also 500/100 largest) and 1,000 largest European stocks; trading-cost estimates from the Keim-Madhavan model and Nomura Securities data. Accepted manuscript: https://repub.eur.nl/pub/25718/AnotherLook_2011.pdf
sample_period: US January 1990 - December 2009; Europe January 1995 - December 2009.
methodology: Daily sort into quintiles on past-week (5-day) returns, skip one day, equal-weighted long losers/short winners measured against the equal-weighted universe, rebalanced daily; stock-level net returns; a 'smart' rule only exits when a stock leaves the bottom/top 50%.
reported_effect: 1,500 largest US stocks: 61.7 bp per week gross but -66.1 bp (Keim-Madhavan) or -103.7 bp (Nomura) per week net, with 677% weekly turnover. Restricting to the largest stocks gives up to 30 bp per week net; adding the low-turnover rule gives up to 50 bp per week net in the US and up to 20 bp per week net in Europe.
transaction_costs: Central: stock-level commission plus market-impact estimates (Keim-Madhavan, Nomura), floored at zero; trade sizes up to $1 million per stock examined.
survivorship_treatment: Universe = largest stocks at each date (index membership); delisting handling not described in text reviewed.
out_of_sample_evidence: Authors report positive net returns after decimalization within their sample. Medhat & Schmeling (2022, https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhab055) find that for 1963-2018 the conventional value-weighted monthly reversal's cost (0.56% per month) subsumes its gross return.
known_criticisms: Keim-Madhavan parameters were estimated on 1991-1993 NYSE/AMEX institutional trades (authors discuss this); daily rebalancing at closing prices; returns measured relative to the equal-weighted universe.
replication_status: No independent replication of the net figures found.
post_publication_decay: Medhat & Schmeling (2022) report the low-turnover reversal effect was consistent until 2011 and tapered off afterwards; Robeco researchers (Blitz, van der Grient & Honarvar 2023, SSRN 4575689, summary https://www.robeco.com/en-uk/insights/2023/10/reversing-the-trend-of-short-term-reversal) address concerns about weakening generic reversal and propose industry/factor-momentum-adjusted versions.
relevance_notes: Best template for a lab reversal test: large-cap, buffered, cost-aware weekly reversal on 2016-2024 daily bars, also in residual/industry-adjusted form; charge at least half-spread plus impact and expect gross edges of tens of bp per week to shrink sharply; check whether high-turnover names show continuation instead (Medhat-Schmeling).

title: What happened to the quants in August 2007? Evidence from factors and transactions data
authors: Amir E. Khandani; Andrew W. Lo
venue: Journal of Financial Markets 14(1), 1-46 (first circulated 2007 as 'What Happened To The Quants In August 2007?')
anomaly: The classic daily Lehmann/Lo-MacKinlay contrarian strategy lost most of its profitability between 1995 and 2007, and crowded unwinding of such strategies produced the August 2007 quant losses.
dataset: CRSP daily returns for US common stocks (share codes 10/11, price $5-$2,000) and size deciles; the later version adds S&P 1500 constituents and TAQ data. 2007 version: https://traders.berkeley.edu/papers/What%20Happened%20to%20the%20Quants%20in%20August%202007.pdf
sample_period: January 1995 - August 2007 (2007 version); 1995-2007 in the published version.
methodology: Daily contrarian portfolio with weights proportional to minus each stock's prior-day return relative to the equal-weighted market, normalized to $1 long/$1 short; year-by-year average daily returns by size decile; event study of August 2007.
reported_effect: Gross average daily return 1.38% in 1995, 0.44% in 2000 and 0.13% in 2007 (to 31 August), while daily volatility rose from 0.40% to 0.72%; in 1995 the smallest size decile earned 3.57% per day versus 0.04% per day in the largest decile.
transaction_costs: Not treated; the authors stress these returns are unrealistic because they ignore costs, price impact and short-sale constraints.
survivorship_treatment: Daily universe; stocks leave when they delist, change share code or exit the price range (no survivor-only filter).
out_of_sample_evidence: This is out-of-sample evidence for Lehmann (1990) and Lo & MacKinlay (1990).
known_criticisms: Gross daily-rebalanced returns are not implementable; the decline mixes competition, market-structure change and lower volatility.
replication_status: The published version confirms the decline on S&P 1500 components (pre-2002 years above, 2002-onward below the full-sample average).
post_publication_decay: Documents direct decay of the published reversal effect.
relevance_notes: Strong prior that naive daily/weekly reversal in liquid US stocks is near zero gross by 2016-2024 (largest-decile returns were about zero even in 1995-2007); a lab result showing large net large-cap reversal profits should be treated as a probable bug (look-ahead, bid-ask bounce in closing prints).

title: Short-term Momentum
authors: Mamdouh Medhat; Maik Schmeling
anomaly: Conditioning last month's return on share turnover: low-turnover stocks show short-term reversal, but high-turnover stocks show short-term momentum.
dataset: CRSP/Compustat NYSE/AMEX/Nasdaq non-financial common stocks; international data for robustness. Accepted version: https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/31278/1/MS_short_term_mom_v27.pdf
methodology: Conditional decile double sorts with NYSE breakpoints, first on prior-month return, then on prior-month turnover; value-weighted monthly portfolios; factor regressions; costs from CRSP half-spreads times turnover.
reported_effect: Winner-minus-loser within the highest-turnover decile (STMOM) +1.37% per month (t=4.74); within the lowest-turnover decile (STREV*) -1.41% per month (t=-7.13); value-weighted, gross.
transaction_costs: Treated with half-spreads: STMOM costs about 0.37% per month, leaving 1.00% net (t=3.47); large/megacap STMOM about 0.60% per month net; STREV* costs 1.94% per month and the conventional STREV 0.56% per month, each subsuming the gross return.
survivorship_treatment: CRSP universe; delisting handling not verified.
out_of_sample_evidence: Authors report the pattern internationally; STREV* returns were consistent until 2011 then tapered off; STMOM was weak only in 1975-79.
known_criticisms: Turnover as conditioning variable is sensitive to market structure; half-spread costs omit price impact; recent, little independent replication.
replication_status: No independent replication reviewed.
post_publication_decay: Too recent; within sample the reversal leg weakened after 2011.
relevance_notes: For a liquid-stock lab the prior at the one-month horizon in high-turnover large caps is continuation, not reversal; test both signs conditional on turnover using daily data aggregated monthly; costs for large caps were modest in their estimates.

title: Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency
authors: Narasimhan Jegadeesh; Sheridan Titman
anomaly: Stocks with high returns over the past 3-12 months keep outperforming past losers over the next 3-12 months, with partial reversal in years 2-3.
dataset: CRSP NYSE and AMEX stocks.
methodology: Overlapping J-month formation / K-month holding equal-weighted decile portfolios, with and without a one-week skip; risk adjustment, decomposition of profits, event-time returns up to 36 months.
reported_effect: Best strategy (12-month formation, 3-month holding, 1-week skip) earns 1.49% per month gross (1.31% without the skip); 6-month formation earns about 1% per month across holding periods. Momentum loses about 7% on average each January.
transaction_costs: Treated: with 0.5% one-way costs and 84.8% semiannual turnover the risk-adjusted return is 9.29% per year, significant.
survivorship_treatment: CRSP NYSE/AMEX historical universe; explicit delisting handling not described in text reviewed.
out_of_sample_evidence: Jegadeesh & Titman (2001, JF 56(2), 699-720, https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v56y2001i2p699-720.html) report momentum profits continued in the 1990s. Blitz, Huij & Martens (2011) report total-return momentum earned -8.5% per year in 2000-2009.
known_criticisms: Crash risk in market rebounds (Daniel & Moskowitz 2016); high turnover and trading costs (literature reviewed in Novy-Marx & Velikov 2016); strong January seasonality.
replication_status: Chen-Zimmermann: Mom12m (original 1.31% per month, t=3.74) and Mom6m (0.84%, t=2.44) are clear predictors (https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv). HXZ 2017 WP (VW, NYSE breakpoints, 1967-2014): 6-month momentum earns 0.82% (t=3.49) and 0.55% (t=2.90) per month at 6- and 12-month holding versus 1.1% and 0.9% in JT; 11-month momentum earns 1.19% (t=4.06) at 1-month holding - replicated but smaller.
post_publication_decay: Survived the 1990s (JT 2001), negative in 2000-2009 and crashed in March-May 2009 (Daniel & Moskowitz). Novy-Marx & Velikov (2016, https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhv063) still find VW decile momentum 1.33% gross and 0.68% net per month (t=2.45) over 1963-2013.
relevance_notes: Easy to test with daily data 2016-2024 (monthly rebalancing). Expect modest, unstable value-weighted spreads in large caps, crash exposure after market rebounds, and costs of roughly 0.6% per month on a decile book; test residual and volatility-managed variants alongside.

title: Momentum crashes
authors: Kent Daniel; Tobias J. Moskowitz
anomaly: Momentum's rare but severe crashes are partly forecastable: they occur in 'panic' states after market declines with high volatility, coinciding with market rebounds when past losers surge.
dataset: CRSP US equities (value-weighted top-minus-bottom decile on prior 12-month returns skipping the last month), plus international equities and other asset classes. NBER WP: https://www.nber.org/papers/w20439
methodology: Conditional analysis of winner-minus-loser (WML) returns in bear markets and high-volatility states; option-like payoff of losers; dynamic weighting using forecasts of momentum's mean and variance.
reported_effect: WML Sharpe ratio 0.71 vs 0.40 for the market and CAPM alpha 22.3% per year (t=8.5) over 1927-2013, gross. July-August 1932: losers +232% vs winners +32%; March-May 2009: losers +163% vs winners +8%. The dynamic strategy roughly doubles alpha and Sharpe of static momentum; dynamic momentum across all markets/asset classes has a Sharpe of 1.18.
transaction_costs: Not treated (returns explicitly exclude transaction costs).
survivorship_treatment: CRSP universe; portfolio membership fixed within the month except for delisting.
out_of_sample_evidence: Authors report robustness across time periods, international equity markets and other asset classes.
known_criticisms: The dynamic strategy scales exposure strongly (higher turnover and leverage) and costs are excluded.
replication_status: Crash behavior corroborated in other datasets, e.g. Blitz, Huij & Martens (2011) on 2009.
post_publication_decay: No post-2016 estimate reviewed.
relevance_notes: Any momentum test on 2016-2024 should report rebound months separately and treat crash conditioning (trailing market drawdown plus realized volatility) as a pre-registered overlay hypothesis tested out-of-sample, not a tuned parameter.

title: Residual momentum
authors: David Blitz; Joop Huij; Martin Martens
anomaly: Ranking stocks on Fama-French residual (stock-specific) returns gives momentum with about half the volatility and roughly double the Sharpe ratio of total-return momentum.
dataset: CRSP domestic primary NYSE/AMEX/Nasdaq stocks; Fama-French factors. Accepted manuscript: https://repub.eur.nl/pub/22252/ResidualMomentum-2011.pdf
sample_period: January 1930 - December 2009 (CRSP data from 1926 used for estimation).
methodology: Monthly FF3 regressions over 36-month rolling windows (complete history required); rank on 12-1 month residual returns standardized by residual volatility; top-minus-bottom deciles versus total-return momentum; conditional Grundy-Martin-style factor alphas.
reported_effect: One-month holding: total-return momentum 10.26% per year with 22.70% volatility (FF alpha 7.98%); residual momentum has about 1% per year higher return, 2.9% per year higher alpha and 12.49% volatility, so roughly double the Sharpe ratio (gross). 2000-2009: total-return momentum -8.5% per year vs residual momentum +4.7% per year.
transaction_costs: Not modelled; authors argue costs should be lower because residual momentum is less concentrated in small caps.
survivorship_treatment: CRSP universe; the 36-month complete-history requirement excludes young firms; delisting handling not verified.
out_of_sample_evidence: HXZ 2017 WP (https://conference.nber.org/conf_papers/f102921/f102921.pdf, VW, NYSE breakpoints, 1967-2014): 6-month residual momentum 0.49% per month (t=3.86) at 6-month holding; 11-month residual momentum 0.67% (t=3.91) at 1-month holding.
known_criticisms: Gross of costs; depends on the factor model and lookback chosen; data-hungry (36-month regressions).
replication_status: Chen-Zimmermann: ResidualMomentum is a clear predictor (original equal-weighted decile 0.93% per month, t=8.22; https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv); HXZ: significant.
post_publication_decay: No signal-specific post-2011 estimate reviewed.
relevance_notes: Good candidate for a liquid-US daily-data lab: lower volatility and less small-cap dependence. Estimate betas point-in-time with rolling windows (needs data from 2013 for 2016 signals) and compare with raw 12-1 momentum on 2016-2024 net of costs.

title: The 52-Week High and Momentum Investing
authors: Thomas J. George; Chuan-Yang Hwang
anomaly: Stocks trading near their 52-week high outperform stocks far below it; nearness to the 52-week high dominates past returns as a predictor and its predicted returns do not reverse in the long run.
dataset: All CRSP stocks. Author copy: https://www.bauer.uh.edu/tgeorge/papers/gh4-paper.pdf
methodology: (6,6) strategies with equal-weighted top/bottom 30% portfolios ranked on price/52-week high, compared with Jegadeesh-Titman individual and Moskowitz-Grinblatt industry momentum; regressions skip a month to control bid-ask bounce.
reported_effect: Winner-minus-loser 0.45% per month (t=2.00) for the 52-week-high strategy (JT momentum 0.48%, t=2.35; industry momentum 0.45%, t=3.43), gross. Excluding January 1.23% per month (t=7.06); January only -8.27% (t=-5.49).
transaction_costs: not treated
survivorship_treatment: All CRSP stocks; delisting handling not verified.
out_of_sample_evidence: HXZ 2017 WP (https://conference.nber.org/conf_papers/f102921/f102921.pdf, VW, NYSE breakpoints): 6-month holding 52-week-high decile spread 0.57% per month (t=2.02); 1- and 12-month holding versions insignificant.
known_criticisms: Large January reversal; equal-weighted; only marginal in value-weighted NYSE-breakpoint replication.
replication_status: Chen-Zimmermann: High52 original evidence 'likely' (t=2.0) with good reproduction quality (https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv); HXZ: marginal.
post_publication_decay: No signal-specific estimate reviewed; default McLean-Pontiff prior.
relevance_notes: Trivial to compute from daily highs (point-in-time 252-day window). Expect weak value-weighted results in large caps and a January penalty; compare with and combine with 12-1 momentum rather than test in isolation.

title: Momentum Strategies
authors: Louis K. C. Chan; Narasimhan Jegadeesh; Josef Lakonishok
anomaly: Past returns and past earnings news (standardized unexpected earnings, announcement abnormal returns, analyst forecast revisions) each predict drifts in future returns, consistent with slow incorporation of information.
dataset: NYSE/AMEX/Nasdaq stocks; CRSP, Compustat, I/B/E/S (summary: https://rpc.cfainstitute.org/-/media/documents/article/cfa-digest/1997/dig-v27-n3-113-pdf.pdf).
methodology: Equal-weighted decile portfolios on prior 6-month return, SUE, abnormal return around the latest announcement, and analyst forecast revisions; buy-and-hold returns over 6-36 months; two-way sorts and cross-sectional regressions; size and book-to-market adjustments.
reported_effect: As quoted by HXZ: high-minus-low decile 6- and 12-month buy-and-hold returns of 6.8% and 7.5% (SUE), 5.9% and 8.3% (announcement abnormal return), and 7.7% and 9.7% (analyst revisions), equal-weighted, gross. Earnings-news effects are shorter-lived than price momentum.
transaction_costs: Not treated in the original. Novy-Marx & Velikov (2016, https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhv063) report VW decile PEAD(SUE) 0.72% gross / 0.26% net per month (t=1.60) and PEAD(CAR3) 0.91% / 0.34% (t=2.41).
out_of_sample_evidence: HXZ 2017 WP (https://conference.nber.org/conf_papers/f102921/f102921.pdf, 1967-2014, VW, NYSE breakpoints): SUE 0.19% per month at 6-month holding (t=1.65) and 0.11% at 12-month (t=1.00), insignificant; announcement return 0.74% at 1-month (t=5.85) and 0.30% at 6-month (t=3.24); revisions 0.81% at 1-month (t=3.28) and 0.54% at 6-month (t=2.49).
known_criticisms: Equal weighting inflates magnitudes relative to value-weighted NYSE-breakpoint versions.
replication_status: Chen-Zimmermann reproduce AnnouncementReturn (original regression t=9.25) and REV6 (t=4.07) as clear predictors (https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv); HXZ replicate the announcement-return and revision signals but not SUE at 6/12 months.
post_publication_decay: Martineau (2022) finds analyst-surprise drift absent for non-microcaps since 2006 (see PEAD entries).
relevance_notes: Needs point-in-time analyst estimates and announcement dates; with price data only, the announcement-window abnormal return is the most testable piece. Expect small value-weighted effects in 2016-2024 large caps.

title: A tug of war: Overnight versus intraday expected returns
authors: Dong Lou; Christopher Polk; Spyros Skouras
anomaly: Momentum-type strategies and short-term reversal earn their premia overnight, while most other anomalies (value, profitability, investment, beta, IVOL, issuance, accruals, turnover) earn theirs intraday, with an opposite-signed premium in the other period.
dataset: CRSP/Compustat US stocks; TAQ to define the open as the VWAP of 9:30-10:00 am; Thomson Reuters Tick History for nine international markets. Author copy: https://personal.lse.ac.uk/polk/research/TugOfWar.pdf
methodology: Split close-to-close returns into overnight (prior close to 9:30-10:00 VWAP) and intraday parts; value-weighted decile long-short strategies on 14 characteristics; CAPM alphas of each part; persistence of overnight/intraday returns up to 60 months.
reported_effect: Monthly CAPM alphas (VW deciles): price momentum 0.98% overnight (t=3.84) vs -0.02% intraday; short-term reversal 0.93% overnight vs -1.05% intraday; IVOL strategy -1.46% overnight vs +2.48% intraday; SUE 0.56% overnight (t=3.20). Overnight momentum Sharpe 0.77 vs 0.31 close-to-close, gross.
transaction_costs: Not treated; the authors note costs make exploiting these patterns much less attractive.
survivorship_treatment: CRSP universe; excludes observations with fewer than 1,000 shares traded in the first half hour.
out_of_sample_evidence: Authors find similar overnight and intraday continuation in nine international markets.
known_criticisms: The 'open' is a 30-minute VWAP rather than the opening auction; a twice-daily book doubles turnover; the decomposition describes when premia accrue rather than giving a standalone strategy.
replication_status: No independent replication reviewed.
post_publication_decay: No post-2013 estimate reviewed.
relevance_notes: Daily OHLC allows an approximate split using the official open (which differs from their VWAP). Use as attribution for the lab's own anomaly P&L (e.g., does momentum accrue overnight?), not as an overnight-only trading strategy.

title: Market intraday momentum
authors: Lei Gao; Yufeng Han; Sophia Zhengzi Li; Guofu Zhou
anomaly: The S&P 500 ETF's first half-hour return (measured from the previous close) predicts its last half-hour return.
dataset: High-frequency SPY data (TAQ) plus ten other actively traded domestic and international ETFs. WP copy: https://assets.super.so/e46b77e7-ee08-445e-b43f-4ffd88ae0a0e/files/ee7dac49-530b-4950-b5d0-e0b5eee08f2e.pdf
methodology: Predictive regressions of the last half-hour return on the first (and twelfth) half-hour returns, in and out of sample; a timing strategy long/short SPY over the last half hour by the sign of the first half-hour return; conditioning on volatility, volume, recessions and macro-news days.
reported_effect: Predictive R2 of 1.6% for the first half-hour return; the timing strategy earns 6.67% per year with 6.19% standard deviation (Sharpe 1.08) vs buy-and-hold 6.04% with 20.57% (Sharpe 0.29), gross. Predictability is stronger on volatile, high-volume, recession and macro-news days (R2 11.0% on news-release days in one test).
transaction_costs: Treated after decimalization using 3:30 pm bid/ask (commissions ignored): 4.46% per year after costs, 2.47 points below pre-cost, from July 2001; from 2005, 6.52% after vs 7.96% before costs.
survivorship_treatment: Not applicable (index ETF).
out_of_sample_evidence: Baltussen, Da, Lammers & Martens (2021 JFE, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2021.04.029; 60+ futures, 1974-2020) confirm market intraday momentum broadly, but the overnight-plus-first-half-hour predictor has a negative out-of-sample R2 (-1.71%) in their extended equity-index futures sample, while the rest-of-day return predicts well.
known_criticisms: Requires intraday prices (10:00 am and 3:30 pm); the effect is linked to time-varying gamma-hedging and leveraged-ETF rebalancing flows (Baltussen et al.), so it can weaken or strengthen with dealer positioning.
replication_status: Partially replicated: intraday momentum confirmed, the specific first-half-hour predictor not robust out-of-sample (Baltussen et al. 2021).
post_publication_decay: No direct post-2018 estimate reviewed.
relevance_notes: Not testable with daily bars (needs 10:00 and 3:30 pm prices); open-to-close proxies are a different signal. Out of scope unless intraday index data are added.

title: Hedging demand and market intraday momentum
authors: Guido Baltussen; Zhi Da; Sten Lammers; Martin Martens
anomaly: Across 60+ futures, the return in the last 30 minutes before the close is positively predicted by the return over the rest of the day, linked to short-gamma hedging by option dealers and leveraged ETFs.
dataset: Intraday returns on more than 60 futures (equity indexes, bonds, commodities, currencies). Author copy: https://www3.nd.edu/~zda/intramom.pdf
methodology: Predictive regressions of last-30-minute returns on the rest-of-day return and on the overnight-plus-first-half-hour return; expanding-window out-of-sample R2; conditioning on net gamma exposure.
reported_effect: Rest-of-day return out-of-sample R2 2.22% (2.88% combined with other intraday predictors) vs -1.71% for the overnight-plus-first-half-hour predictor in the extended equity-index futures sample; predictability is stronger when net gamma exposure is more negative and reverts over the next days.
transaction_costs: Not considered in the main tests; the authors note a positive net Sharpe for S&P 500 futures assuming a one-tick cost.
survivorship_treatment: Not applicable (futures).
out_of_sample_evidence: Out-of-sample R2 reported within the paper (expanding windows).
known_criticisms: Effect depends on time-varying dealer and leveraged-ETF gamma; requires intraday execution near the close.
replication_status: Independent extension of Gao et al. (2018); supports intraday momentum but not their specific predictor.
relevance_notes: Out of scope for daily bars; recorded because it qualifies Gao et al. (2018) and shows the predictor choice matters.

title: Maxing out: Stocks as lotteries and the cross-section of expected returns
authors: Turan G. Bali; Nusret Cakici; Robert F. Whitelaw
anomaly: Stocks with the highest maximum daily return over the past month (lottery-like stocks) earn low subsequent returns.
dataset: CRSP NYSE/AMEX/Nasdaq stocks, daily and monthly. NBER WP: https://www.nber.org/papers/w14804
methodology: Monthly decile sorts on MAX (maximum daily return in the prior month), value- and equal-weighted; bivariate sorts and Fama-MacBeth regressions controlling size, book-to-market, momentum, reversal, liquidity, skewness and idiosyncratic volatility.
reported_effect: Value-weighted decile 10 minus 1: -1.03% per month raw and -1.18% per month four-factor alpha (t=-4.71), gross; using the average of the five highest daily returns gives -1.23% and -1.32%. Including MAX reverses the negative IVOL-return relation.
transaction_costs: Not treated; the authors note high-MAX stocks are small and illiquid, so costs may seriously impede implementation.
survivorship_treatment: CRSP universe; delisting handling not verified.
out_of_sample_evidence: HXZ 2017 WP (https://conference.nber.org/conf_papers/f102921/f102921.pdf, 1967-2014, NYSE breakpoints, VW): MAX decile spread -0.34% per month (t=-1.14), insignificant; decile returns stay flat until the top decile (0.64%).
known_criticisms: Effect concentrated in small, illiquid stocks; sensitive to breakpoints and weighting; overlaps with IVOL and short-term reversal.
replication_status: Chen-Zimmermann: MaxRet clear in the original (VW, 1.03%, t=2.83) with good reproduction (https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv); HXZ: fails with NYSE breakpoints.
post_publication_decay: No separate estimate; HXZ's failure with NYSE breakpoints suggests little to harvest in large caps.
relevance_notes: Trivial to compute from daily data; in a liquid large-cap universe expect a weak or null spread. More useful as an avoid/short screen or a control variable than as a standalone strategy.

title: The Cross-Section of Volatility and Expected Returns
authors: Andrew Ang; Robert J. Hodrick; Yuhang Xing; Xiaoyan Zhang
anomaly: Stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility relative to the Fama-French three-factor model have abysmally low subsequent returns (and stocks with high sensitivity to aggregate volatility innovations earn low returns).
dataset: CRSP NYSE/AMEX/Nasdaq stocks (daily returns); VIX for aggregate-volatility tests. NBER WP: https://www.nber.org/papers/w10852
methodology: Monthly quintile sorts on prior-month idiosyncratic volatility of daily FF3 residuals; value-weighted portfolios held one month (plus 12/1/12 variants); FF3 alphas; controls for size, book-to-market, momentum, liquidity, dispersion and coskewness.
reported_effect: Quintile 5 minus 1: -1.06% per month raw and -1.31% per month FF3 alpha (t=-7.00), value-weighted, gross.
transaction_costs: Not treated originally. Novy-Marx & Velikov (2016, https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhv063): VW decile IVOL strategy (1963-2013) earns 0.63% per month gross but 0.11% net (t=0.37) after 0.52% per month costs.
survivorship_treatment: CRSP universe; delisting handling not verified.
out_of_sample_evidence: Mixed: HXZ 2017 WP (https://conference.nber.org/conf_papers/f102921/f102921.pdf) find the NYSE-breakpoint VW decile spread -0.51% per month (t=-1.62), insignificant (but -1.28%, t=-3.48, with all-stock breakpoints); Bali & Cakici (2008 JFQA 43(1), https://ideas.repec.org/a/cup/jfinqa/v43y2008i01p29-58_00.html) find no robust relation across weighting schemes, breakpoints and samples.
known_criticisms: Sensitive to breakpoints, weighting and microcaps; partly subsumed by MAX (Bali et al. 2011); Lou-Polk-Skouras (2019) show the premium accrues intraday with an offsetting overnight component.
replication_status: Chen-Zimmermann: IdioVol3F clear in the original (VW quintiles 1.06%, t=3.1) and reproduced (https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv); HXZ: fails with NYSE breakpoints and value weights.
post_publication_decay: No separate estimate; net-of-cost value near zero (Novy-Marx & Velikov 2016).
relevance_notes: Easy to compute from daily data; in a liquid universe use low-IVOL as a defensive/risk overlay hypothesis and expect little net long-short alpha in 2016-2024.

title: Betting against beta
authors: Andrea Frazzini; Lasse Heje Pedersen
anomaly: A beta-neutral portfolio long leveraged low-beta stocks and short de-leveraged high-beta stocks (BAB) earns significant risk-adjusted returns, attributed to leverage constraints.
dataset: CRSP US common stocks, 19 other developed equity markets, Treasuries, corporate bonds, futures. NBER WP: https://www.nber.org/papers/w16601
sample_period: US equities 1926-2009 in the December-2010 working paper; Chen-Zimmermann record the published US sample as 1929-2012.
methodology: Pre-ranking betas from rolling regressions, shrunk toward the cross-sectional mean (weight 0.5); stocks rank-weighted into low- and high-beta portfolios, each rescaled to a beta of one; monthly rebalancing; 1-, 3-, 4- and 5-factor alphas.
reported_effect: Working paper: US BAB Sharpe ratio 0.75 (1926-2009); FF3 alpha 0.69% per month (t=6.55), four-factor 0.55% (t=5.12), five-factor 0.46% (t=2.93), gross; positive in each 20-year subperiod.
transaction_costs: Not treated by FP. Novy-Marx & Velikov (2022 JFE 143(1), 80-106, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2021.05.023) find BAB positive after transaction costs but earned through tilts toward profitability and investment.
survivorship_treatment: CRSP universe; delisting handling not verified.
out_of_sample_evidence: FP report BAB in 19 other countries and other asset classes. JKP (2023) note HXZ's raw-return 'failure' of low-beta is expected because theory predicts positive alpha with near-zero raw return.
known_criticisms: Novy-Marx & Velikov (2022): performance is driven by non-standard construction that effectively equal-weights; on average $1.05 per $1 of BAB is committed to stocks in the bottom 1% of market cap, and predictable beta-estimation biases drive the evidence for the theory. HXZ: FP-beta deciles earn about -0.2% per month raw, insignificant.
replication_status: Chen-Zimmermann list BetaFP as 'likely' with 'distant' reproduction quality because of the nonstandard construction (https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv); HXZ raw-return beta sorts insignificant.
post_publication_decay: No post-2014 estimate reviewed.
relevance_notes: With value weights in liquid US stocks expect much weaker results than published BAB (microcap dependence); test a conventional value-weighted, beta-neutral low-minus-high beta book, report alphas including profitability/investment factors, and charge financing for the levered long leg.

title: The Earnings Announcement Premium and Trading Volume
authors: Owen Lamont; Andrea Frazzini (author order on the NBER paper; commonly cited as Frazzini & Lamont 2007)
anomaly: Stocks earn higher returns in months when they are expected to announce earnings; the premium is tied to announcement-period volume surges and small-investor buying.
dataset: CRSP common stocks; Compustat announcement dates; expected announcement months predicted from prior-year timing.
methodology: Calendar-time portfolios long expected announcers and short expected non-announcers each month; CAPM/factor regressions; sorts on past announcement-period volume; NYSE size deciles.
reported_effect: Long-short 61 bp per month (about 7% per year, t>5) with annual Sharpe 0.94; 40-92 bp per month across subperiods; monthly variants earn 7%-18% per year; large caps earn a large significant premium (gross).
transaction_costs: Not treated; the authors call it more attractive than other factors 'before considering trading costs', and the book turns over most positions monthly.
survivorship_treatment: CRSP universe; requires a prior year of announcements to predict dates (excludes new listings).
out_of_sample_evidence: Barber, De George, Lehavy & Trueman (2013) find the premium in 46 countries over 1991-2010.
known_criticisms: Expected (not actual) dates are needed to avoid look-ahead; monthly windows are coarse; the premium may compensate announcement risk.
replication_status: Out-of-sample international confirmation by Barber et al. (2013); not part of Chen-Zimmermann's characteristic set.
post_publication_decay: No post-2007 US estimate reviewed.
relevance_notes: Testable with daily data and a point-in-time earnings calendar (2016-2024): long expected announcers around the window vs non-announcers; very high turnover makes costs decisive; focus on large caps where the premium was reported to hold.

title: The earnings announcement premium around the globe
authors: Brad M. Barber; Emmanuel T. De George; Reuven Lehavy; Brett Trueman
anomaly: The higher return of stocks in their expected earnings-announcement months exists across countries.
dataset: About 200,000 annual earnings announcements from 46 countries (I/B/E/S, Thomson Datastream and other sources). WP: https://en-coller.tau.ac.il/sites/nihul_en.tau.ac.il/files/media_server/Recanati/management/seminars/account/barber.pdf
sample_period: Expected announcement months 1991 - 2010 (dates from 1990-2009 used to form expectations).
methodology: Monthly long expected announcers / short expected non-announcers (expectation from prior-year timing); pooled and within-country calendar-time and regression tests with return-factor controls; cross-country link to the announcement-time rise in idiosyncratic volatility.
reported_effect: Working-paper version (June 2011): long-short 66.8 bp per month (8.02% annualized); announcement-month returns exceed non-announcement returns by over 11% annually after controls; significant in 16 of 20 years and individually in 9 of 20 countries; premium for the smallest stocks exceeds the largest by about 6% annually (gross).
transaction_costs: not treated
out_of_sample_evidence: Itself an out-of-sample (international, later-period) test of the US premium.
known_criticisms: Uses annual announcements; premium larger in small stocks, contrary to Frazzini-Lamont's US size result.
replication_status: Confirms the US evidence internationally.
post_publication_decay: No post-2013 estimate reviewed.
relevance_notes: Suggests a robust but small-stock-tilted premium; in a liquid US universe expect a smaller premium than the 46-country average.

title: Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift: Delayed Price Response or Risk Premium?
authors: Victor L. Bernard; Jacob K. Thomas
anomaly: Stock prices keep drifting in the direction of quarterly earnings surprises for about 60 trading days after the announcement.
dataset: Quarterly earnings and stock returns for US-listed firms; time-series (Foster 1977-type) earnings expectations.
methodology: Standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) from a time-series expectation model, deflated by the standard deviation of forecast errors; decile portfolios; abnormal returns over the 60 trading days after announcements; tests of risk-based explanations.
reported_effect: Extreme good (bad) news deciles drift about +2% (-2%) over 60 trading days, i.e. about 4% per quarter (18% annualized) for the zero-investment spread, gross (Fink 2020 review, https://static.uni-graz.at/fileadmin/sowi/Working_Paper/2020-04_Fink.pdf). The spread is positive in 41 of 48 quarters, including 11 of 16 with negative NYSE returns (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post%E2%80%93earnings-announcement_drift).
transaction_costs: Not a cost study. Later work is split: some studies find near-zero profits after frictions (Chordia et al. 2009; Ng et al. 2008), others significant (Fink 2020 review); Novy-Marx & Velikov (2016) report VW PEAD(SUE) 0.26% per month net (t=1.60).
out_of_sample_evidence: Drift persisted for two decades after publication and across markets (Fink 2020), but Martineau (2022) finds it absent for non-microcaps since 2006 and microcaps since 2016.
known_criticisms: Concentrated in small, illiquid, high-cost stocks; magnitude depends on the expectation model (time-series vs analyst); risk vs limits-to-arbitrage explanations debated.
replication_status: Chen-Zimmermann reproduce EarningsSurprise (Foster-Olsen-Shevlin 1984) as a clear predictor (https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv); HXZ 2017 WP: SUE 0.47% per month at 1-month holding (t=3.42) but insignificant at 6/12 months.
post_publication_decay: Strong: Martineau (2022); Subrahmanyam (2025, summarized at https://anderson-review.ucla.edu/is-post-earnings-announcement-drift-a-thing-again/) finds an announcement-return drift factor barely significant in all stocks (t=2.18) and insignificant excluding microcaps (t=1.43) over February 2001 - December 2024.
relevance_notes: For a liquid-US 2016-2024 lab the prior is no PEAD; test with point-in-time surprises (announcement-window returns are the cleanest daily-data proxy) and expect net results indistinguishable from zero.

title: Rest in Peace Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
authors: Charles Martineau
anomaly: Decline evidence: post-earnings-announcement drift has disappeared because prices now fully reflect earnings surprises on the announcement date.
dataset: US stocks with I/B/E/S analyst surprises (and random-walk surprises), split into all-but-microcap (above NYSE 20th size percentile) and microcap. Draft: https://cfr.ivo-welch.info/published/papers/martineau2021rest.pdf
methodology: Daily cumulative returns over 60 trading days after announcements conditional on surprise; announcement-date response to surprises over time; subperiod tests of whether surprises predict post-announcement returns by size group.
reported_effect: Announcement-date price response to surprises in 2016-2019 is about six times (all-but-microcap) and three times (microcap) that of 1984-1990; analyst surprises fail to positively predict 60-day post-announcement returns for all-but-microcap stocks since 2006 and for microcaps since 2016.
transaction_costs: Not applicable (documents absence of gross drift).
out_of_sample_evidence: Subrahmanyam (2025; https://anderson-review.ucla.edu/is-post-earnings-announcement-drift-a-thing-again/) finds drift insignificant ex-microcaps over 2001-2024; two 2025 papers (Dickerson-Julliard-Mueller; Hirshleifer-Peng-Wang) argue drift persists, which Subrahmanyam attributes to microcaps and controls.
known_criticisms: Contested by the 2025 papers above using alternative measures.
replication_status: Consistent with HXZ's weak value-weighted SUE results and Chordia-Subrahmanyam-Tong's attenuation evidence.
post_publication_decay: This paper is itself the decay evidence for PEAD.
relevance_notes: Strong prior: no PEAD in liquid US stocks after 2006. A positive lab result in 2016-2024 large caps should trigger a point-in-time audit (surprise timestamps, before-open vs after-close announcements).

title: The Pre-FOMC Announcement Drift
authors: David O. Lucca; Emanuel Moench
anomaly: US equities earn large average excess returns in the 24 hours before scheduled FOMC announcements.
dataset: S&P 500 intraday and daily returns, international equity indices, Treasuries and money-market futures. Staff report: https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/staff_reports/sr512.pdf
methodology: Average excess returns in the 2 pm-to-2 pm window before scheduled announcements versus other days; close-to-close FOMC-day returns; robustness to outliers and data snooping; conditioning on yield-curve slope, implied volatility and past pre-FOMC returns.
reported_effect: SPX rose 49 bp on average in the 24 hours before announcements (t>4.5), about 80% of annual realized excess returns since 1994; holding only that window gives an annualized Sharpe of 1.14. Close-to-close FOMC-day excess return about 33 bp (Sharpe 0.84); 1980-1993 meeting days 20 bp; none before 1980 (gross).
transaction_costs: not treated
survivorship_treatment: Not applicable (index).
out_of_sample_evidence: Kurov, Wolfe & Gilbert (2021 FRL 40, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.frl.2020.101781; sample to December 2019) find the drift essentially disappeared after 2015.
known_criticisms: Only eight scheduled meetings per year; no accepted explanation; later disappearance points to regime dependence (press conferences, uncertainty).
replication_status: Out-of-sample through 2019 (Kurov et al. 2021): not robust after 2015.
post_publication_decay: Essentially disappeared after 2015.
relevance_notes: Testable with daily index/ETF data via close-to-close FOMC-day returns (the 2 pm window needs intraday data). Prior for 2016-2024 is near-zero drift, and about 72 scheduled meetings give very low power.

title: The disappearing pre-FOMC announcement drift
authors: Alexander Kurov; Marketa Halova Wolfe; Thomas Gilbert
anomaly: Out-of-sample decline evidence: the pre-FOMC equity drift essentially disappeared after 2015.
dataset: US equity index returns around scheduled FOMC announcements.
methodology: Re-estimate pre-FOMC returns by subperiod, separately for announcements with and without Fed Chair press conferences.
reported_effect: After first appearing before announcements accompanied by press conferences, the drift essentially disappeared after 2015 for meetings with and without press conferences (abstract; post-2015 magnitudes not verified here).
transaction_costs: not treated
survivorship_treatment: Not applicable (index).
out_of_sample_evidence: This paper is the out-of-sample test.
known_criticisms: Short post-2015 window (about 32 scheduled meetings in 2016-2019) limits power; the reduced-uncertainty explanation is conjectural.
post_publication_decay: Documents the disappearance after 2015.
relevance_notes: Sets the lab prior of no pre-FOMC drift for 2016-2019; 2020-2024 is not covered by this paper and is a genuine out-of-sample test window.

title: A Profitable Day Trading Strategy For The U.S. Equity Market
authors: Carlo Zarattini; Andrea Barbon; Andrew Aziz
venue: SSRN Working Paper 4729284 (Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper 24-98); not peer reviewed
anomaly: A 5-minute opening-range-breakout day-trading rule applied only to 'Stocks in Play' (abnormally high relative volume, typically news-driven) earns large, market-uncorrelated returns.
dataset: Intraday data for more than 7,000 US stocks; daily filters: open > $5, 14-day average volume >= 1,000,000 shares, 14-day ATR > $0.50, relative volume >= 100% and top 20 by relative volume (per CXO summary, https://www.cxoadvisory.com/individual-investing/intraday-trading-of-overactive-stocks-via-opening-range-breakout/).
methodology: Each day trade the top 20 Stocks in Play on breakouts of the first 5-minute range, intraday only, with stops at 10% of ATR from entry, 1% of capital risked per trade, a 4x leverage cap and $25,000 starting capital; 15/30/60-minute variants compared.
reported_effect: Top-20 Stocks-in-Play portfolio: total net return over 1,600% (2016-2023), Sharpe 2.81, annualized alpha 36%, versus 198% for the S&P 500 (authors' abstract, https://abarbon.com/papers/a-profitable-day-trading-strategy-for-the-u-s-equity-market).
transaction_costs: Commissions of $0.0035 per share (Interactive Brokers Pro tiered) included; modelling of spread/slippage on breakout entries and stop exits could not be verified, and is critical for a 5-minute strategy.
survivorship_treatment: Not verified (data source and inclusion of delisted names not confirmed in the material reviewed).
out_of_sample_evidence: Only non-peer-reviewed replications found: a QuantConnect re-implementation (1,000 most liquid stocks, 2016 only) reports Sharpe 2.396, beta -0.042, and 68% of 25 parameter variants beating the benchmark Sharpe (https://www.quantconnect.com/research/18444/opening-range-breakout-for-stocks-in-play/); community comments there question other years and fees (about 25% of PnL in one test).
known_criticisms: Practitioner working paper without peer review or independent full-period replication; results hinge on slippage at breakouts/stops, leverage and parameter choices.
replication_status: No peer-reviewed replication; the QuantConnect replication covers 2016 only.
post_publication_decay: Too recent.
relevance_notes: Not testable with daily bars (needs 5-minute data and intraday execution); the lab could only test a daily analogue (relative-volume or gap continuation, open-to-close). Treat headline numbers as unverified.

title: Variance Risk Premiums
authors: Peter Carr; Liuren Wu
anomaly: Option-implied (synthetic variance-swap) rates exceed subsequently realized variance on average - a negative variance risk premium - strongly for major equity indexes but weakly for individual stocks.
dataset: OptionMetrics options on 5 stock indexes and 35 of the most actively traded individual stocks. 2004 WP copy: https://engineering.nyu.edu/sites/default/files/2019-01/CarrReviewofFinStudiesMarch2009-a.pdf
methodology: Synthesize 30-day variance-swap rates from a strip of OTM options; compare with realized variance; Newey-West t-tests (30 lags); CAPM/FF regressions of variance-swap returns.
reported_effect: Mean log variance risk premia exceed -50% per month for the S&P 500 indexes and the Dow (strongly significant); Nasdaq-100 and most single stocks are negative but smaller. In the working paper the log premium is significantly negative for 21 of 35 stocks while the raw premium is insignificant for all but 3 of 35 (Cao & Han 2013 cite the published version as 7 of 35 significantly negative).
transaction_costs: not treated
survivorship_treatment: Fixed set of the 35 most actively traded stocks over the sample (ex-post selection on activity).
out_of_sample_evidence: Driessen, Maenhout & Vilkov (2013 WP, 1996-2012): S&P 500 index realized vol 20.69% vs implied 23.09% (significant), but constituents realized 41.99% vs implied 43.38% (not significant).
known_criticisms: Short sample; ex-post stock selection; single-name variance swaps are costly to replicate with option strips.
replication_status: Index VRP widely replicated; single-stock VRP small or insignificant in Driessen, Maenhout & Vilkov (2009, 2013).
relevance_notes: With 2019-2024 EOD chains the lab can compute model-free implied variance per name and compare with realized; expect a reliable premium for index/ETF options but a small, often insignificant one for single stocks, so single-name short-vol needs a cross-sectional signal rather than a blanket short.

title: Expected Stock Returns and Variance Risk Premia
authors: Tim Bollerslev; George Tauchen; Hao Zhou
anomaly: The aggregate variance risk premium (VIX-squared minus realized variance) predicts future S&P 500 excess returns, most strongly at the quarterly horizon.
dataset: S&P 500 returns; VIX (model-free implied variance); realized variance from 5-minute intraday returns. WP: https://repec.econ.au.dk/repec/creates/rp/08/rp08_48.pdf
methodology: Monthly predictive regressions of 1- to 24-month (overlapping) excess returns on the lagged variance premium, alone and with P/E, dividend yield, default spread and CAY; robust t-statistics.
reported_effect: Quarterly horizon: t=2.86, R2 6.82%; monthly R2 just above 1%; time-series predictability, not a trading backtest (gross).
transaction_costs: not treated
survivorship_treatment: Not applicable (index).
out_of_sample_evidence: Bollerslev, Marrone, Xu & Zhou (2014 JFQA 49(3); FEDS version https://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/feds/2011/201152/index.html) find similar horizon patterns across countries, stronger predictability for a 'global' variance premium, and that finite-sample biases do not explain it.
known_criticisms: Overlapping-return regressions in a short sample (authors caution about R2 interpretation); results depend on high-frequency realized variance and model-free implied variance.
replication_status: International corroboration (Bollerslev et al. 2014).
post_publication_decay: No post-2009 out-of-sample estimate reviewed.
relevance_notes: A market-timing input, not a stock selector. With daily data the lab can compute VIX-squared minus realized variance (the paper stresses intraday RV); 2016-2024 offers only about 36 non-overlapping quarters, so use at most as a pre-registered exposure tilt.

title: Option-Implied Correlations and the Price of Correlation Risk
authors: Joost Driessen; Pascal Maenhout; Grigory Vilkov
anomaly: Single-stock options carry little or no average variance risk premium while index options carry a large one; the gap reflects a priced (negative) correlation risk premium.
dataset: Options on the S&P 500 and DJ30 indexes and all their constituents (model-free implied variance); daily stock returns.
methodology: Compare model-free implied and realized variance for indexes and constituents at 30/60/91 days with stock-by-stock Newey-West tests; implied vs realized correlation; predictive regressions of market returns on implied correlation.
reported_effect: S&P 500 index: realized vol 20.69% vs implied 23.09% (significant). Constituents: realized 41.99% vs implied 43.38% (not significant); a zero 30-day individual premium is not rejected for 503 of 919 stocks (DJ30: 27 of 43). Implied correlation averages 39.5% vs realized 32.5% (S&P 500).
transaction_costs: not treated
survivorship_treatment: Uses all 919 stocks that were S&P 500 constituents at some point in the sample.
out_of_sample_evidence: Extends the 1996-2003 S&P 100 evidence of Driessen, Maenhout & Vilkov (2009) to 2012 with similar conclusions.
known_criticisms: Working paper (publication status not verified); realized variance from daily returns.
replication_status: Consistent with Carr & Wu (2009) single-stock results.
relevance_notes: Key prior for a single-stock options lab: blanket short single-name volatility has no reliable average premium; the premium sits in index options and in the index-vs-constituent (correlation) spread.

title: The Price of Correlation Risk: Evidence from Equity Options
authors: Joost Driessen; Pascal J. Maenhout; Grigory Vilkov
anomaly: Index options are expensive relative to options on index components because market-wide correlation risk is priced; a dispersion trade (sell index volatility, buy constituent volatility) earns high pre-cost returns.
dataset: S&P 100 index options, options on all components, and stock returns.
methodology: Measure index vs individual variance risk premia and implied correlation; test whether correlation-risk exposure explains index and individual option returns; evaluate a strategy selling index straddles and buying component straddles and stocks, with and without frictions.
reported_effect: Index implied volatility averaged 24.7% vs realized 20.8% annualized; no significant variance risk premium in individual options; the correlation strategy earns a risk-adjusted excess return of more than 10% per month before frictions (CXO summary, https://cxoadvisory.com/?p=2110).
transaction_costs: Treated: 'The correlation risk premium cannot be exploited with realistic trading frictions' (abstract).
survivorship_treatment: S&P 100 constituents; details not verified.
out_of_sample_evidence: The authors' 2013 extension (S&P 500/DJ30, 1996-2012) finds implied correlation 39.5% vs realized 32.5% for the S&P 500.
known_criticisms: Requires trading about 100 option series plus index options; frictions eliminate profits; short-correlation books suffer in correlation spikes.
replication_status: Extended by the authors; no independent replication reviewed.
relevance_notes: Feasible in principle with 2019-2024 chains (index ETF options vs constituents) but the authors find frictions eliminate it; treat dispersion as cost-dominated and crash-exposed, and test implied-vs-realized correlation as a signal rather than a harvest.

title: Pairs Trading: Performance of a Relative-Value Arbitrage Rule
authors: Evan Gatev; William N. Goetzmann; K. Geert Rouwenhorst
anomaly: Stocks whose normalized prices moved together historically tend to re-converge after diverging, so a simple long-loser/short-winner pair rule earns excess returns.
dataset: CRSP daily US stock data, excluding stocks with one or more no-trade days in the formation period. NBER WP: https://www.nber.org/papers/w7032
methodology: 12-month formation: match each stock with the partner minimizing the sum of squared deviations of normalized prices; 6-month trading: open when prices diverge by more than two historical standard deviations, close on convergence; top-5/top-20 pair portfolios; bootstrap against random pairs; one-day-wait variant for bid-ask bounce.
reported_effect: Self-financing top-pair portfolios earn average annualized excess returns of up to 11% (published; about 12% in the 1962-1997 version), gross; waiting one day to trade lowers returns by about 200 bp per six-month period.
