transaction_costs: Treated: with a conservative 83 bp per round trip and 2.4 round trips per pair, net profits of 88-168 bp per six-month period remained significant (1999 version); the abstract states profits exceed conservative cost estimates.
survivorship_treatment: Formation-period liquidity screen uses only information up to formation; delisting handling not verified.
out_of_sample_evidence: Do & Faff (2010, FAJ 66(4)) extend to July 1962 - June 2009: top-20 pairs mean excess return fell from 0.86% per month (1962-1988) to 0.37% (1989-2002) and 0.24% (2003-2009).
known_criticisms: Declining profitability; profits concentrated in turbulent periods; short-sale constraints and costs; bid-ask bounce (addressed with the one-day wait).
replication_status: Replicated, with decline, by Do & Faff (2010, 2012).
post_publication_decay: Strong decline after the 1980s (Do & Faff 2010); after costs the baseline rule is unprofitable (Do & Faff 2012).
relevance_notes: Fully testable with daily data. Prior for 2016-2024: near-zero net returns for the distance method in liquid stocks; use within-industry pairs and conservative costs, and expect episodic results (Do & Faff found strength in 2000-02 and 2007-09 turbulence).

title: Does Simple Pairs Trading Still Work?
authors: Binh Do; Robert Faff
anomaly: Decline evidence: the profitability of the Gatev-Goetzmann-Rouwenhorst distance-based pairs rule has fallen steadily, apart from turbulent periods.
dataset: CRSP US stocks.
methodology: Re-run the GGR distance method; attribute the decline to market efficiency versus arbitrage risks (fundamental, noise-trader, synchronization); refined matching using industry homogeneity and number of zero crossings.
reported_effect: Top-20 pairs mean excess return 0.86% per month (1962-1988), 0.37% (1989-2002), 0.24% (2003-2009), gross; strong in the 2000-02 bear market and 2007-09 crisis; refined matching adds 22 bp per month for bank stocks; worsening arbitrage risk explains up to 70% of the drop.
transaction_costs: Not in this paper. Companion Do & Faff (2012, Journal of Financial Research 35(2), 261-287, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-6803.2012.01317.x): baseline strategy unprofitable after trading costs; refined strategies net -0.07% to 0.35% per month (average 0.12%) over July 1962 - December 2009 (CXO summary, https://www.cxoadvisory.com/technical-trading/pairs-trading-net-profitability/).
out_of_sample_evidence: This paper is the out-of-sample extension of GGR.
known_criticisms: Same rule-based limitations as GGR; profits episodic and regime-dependent.
replication_status: Confirms GGR in-sample and documents the decline.
post_publication_decay: Documents the decline over time.
relevance_notes: Prior that naive pairs trading is roughly zero net in recent decades; any lab test should include costs, industry restrictions and results by volatility regime.

title: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?
authors: R. David McLean; Jeffrey Pontiff
anomaly: Meta-study: published cross-sectional predictors earn much less out-of-sample and after publication.
dataset: 97 published characteristics reconstructed from CRSP/Compustat. Copy: https://Www.Gwern.net/doc/economics/2016-mclean.pdf
sample_period: Each predictor's original sample, post-sample pre-publication period and post-publication period; data end in 2013.
methodology: Long-short portfolios replicating each predictor (equal-weighted unless the original study's primary result was value-weighted); panel regressions of monthly returns on out-of-sample and post-publication indicators; interactions with arbitrage costs, trading volume, short interest and correlations.
reported_effect: Average monthly long-short return 0.582% in-sample, 0.402% out-of-sample pre-publication and 0.264% post-publication: 26% lower out-of-sample and 58% lower post-publication, implying about 32% attributable to publication-informed trading (gross).
transaction_costs: Not deducted; post-publication returns are lower for predictors concentrated in liquid, low-idiosyncratic-risk stocks.
out_of_sample_evidence: Chen & Zimmermann (2022) replicate the decay patterns, including on predictors not in MP; JKP (2023) find higher in-sample alphas predict higher post-publication alphas, with somewhat stronger attenuation than their Bayesian model predicts; Jacobs & Muller (2020, as quoted by JKP) find the US is the only country with a reliable post-publication decline.
known_criticisms: Equal-weighted reconstructions include microcaps; some included predictors were not clearly significant originally (Chen & Zimmermann).
replication_status: Replicated by Chen & Zimmermann (2022, Figure 8).
post_publication_decay: Core result: -58% post-publication; decay larger for predictors with higher in-sample returns/t-stats and for predictors built only from price and trading data.
relevance_notes: Default haircut for this lab: 2016-2024 is post-publication for nearly every entry here, so expect roughly half or less of the published gross return, with more decay for technical signals and liquid-stock implementations, before costs.

title: Replicating Anomalies
authors: Kewei Hou; Chen Xue; Lu Zhang
anomaly: Meta-study: most published anomalies are insignificant once microcaps are controlled with NYSE breakpoints and value-weighted returns.
dataset: 452 anomaly variables (447 in the 2017 working paper) from CRSP, Compustat and I/B/E/S across momentum, value, investment, profitability, intangibles and trading-frictions categories. 2017 WP: https://conference.nber.org/conf_papers/f102921/f102921.pdf
sample_period: January 1967 - December 2014 in the June-2017 NBER version; published sample not verified.
methodology: Uniform construction with NYSE breakpoints, value-weighted decile returns, 1/6/12-month holding periods and delisting-return adjustment; single-test |t|>=1.96 and multiple-test 2.78 hurdles; q-factor alphas.
reported_effect: Published abstract: 65% of 452 anomalies fail |t|>=1.96 (82% fail the 2.78 hurdle), including 96% of the trading-frictions category; replicated anomalies are much smaller than originally reported. 2017 WP specifics: short-term reversal -0.26% per month (t=-1.31), IVOL -0.51% (t=-1.62), MAX -0.34% (t=-1.14) insignificant; 6-month momentum 0.82% (t=3.49) and 1-month SUE 0.47% (t=3.42) significant.
transaction_costs: Not deducted (gross).
survivorship_treatment: Delisting returns adjusted following Beaver, McNichols & Price (2007); missing delisting returns replaced with the mean of the same delisting type and exchange over the prior 60 months.
out_of_sample_evidence: Not an out-of-sample study; JKP (2023) contest the conclusions using CAPM alphas and Bayesian multiple testing.
known_criticisms: JKP: raw returns and decile/value-weight choices understate replicability; Chen & Zimmermann: many HXZ variables were never significant in the original papers or are modifications.
replication_status: It is the replication study; disputed by JKP (2023) and Chen & Zimmermann (2022).
post_publication_decay: Not estimated.
relevance_notes: Best guide for a liquid-stock lab: NYSE-breakpoint, value-weighted results approximate what a large-cap book can earn; trading-friction anomalies (reversal, IVOL, MAX, liquidity) should be presumed dead there unless shown otherwise.

title: Open Source Cross-Sectional Asset Pricing
authors: Andrew Y. Chen; Tom Zimmermann
anomaly: Meta-study: using the original papers' methods, nearly all clearly significant published predictors reproduce.
dataset: 319 characteristics from CRSP, Compustat, I/B/E/S, OptionMetrics and other sources with public code and data (https://www.openassetpricing.com, https://github.com/OpenSourceAP/CrossSection/blob/master/SignalDoc.csv). Paper: https://cfr.ivo-welch.info/published/papers/chen2021open.pdf
sample_period: Original papers' sample periods for reproduction tests.
methodology: Reproduce each predictor's long-short portfolio following the original paper and compare t-stats with hand-collected original t-stats; classify predictors by strength of original evidence.
reported_effect: For 161 characteristics clearly significant originally, 98% of reproduced long-short portfolios have t>1.96; regression of reproduced on original t-stats has slope 0.88 and R2 82%; 44 mixed-evidence characteristics average t about 2.
transaction_costs: Not deducted; the authors note Chen & Velikov find effective spreads wipe out most post-publication returns.
out_of_sample_evidence: Replicates McLean-Pontiff: decay rises with in-sample return and t-stat but does not fully eliminate returns (before costs).
known_criticisms: Reproduction with original methods (often equal-weighted) does not establish implementability; microcap-heavy constructions remain.
replication_status: It is the replication. SignalDoc per-signal original stats used in this register: MaxRet t=2.83; IdioVol3F t=3.1; STreversal t=12.44; ResidualMomentum t=8.22; Mom12m t=3.74; High52 'likely' t=2.0; BetaFP 'likely' with distant reproduction; skew1 'likely' t=2.19.
post_publication_decay: Predictability survives publication on average but decays, more for stronger in-sample predictors (gross).
relevance_notes: Use the open-source code and data to cross-check the lab's signal construction and point-in-time timing; reproduction success is not evidence of net profitability in liquid stocks.

title: Is There a Replication Crisis in Finance?
authors: Theis Ingerslev Jensen; Bryan Kelly; Lasse Heje Pedersen
anomaly: Meta-study: most factors replicate in alpha terms, cluster into 13 themes and work out-of-sample in time and across 93 countries.
dataset: 153 factors in 93 countries; US from CRSP (from 1926) with Compustat; data at https://jkpfactors.com, code at https://github.com/bkelly-lab/ReplicationCrisis.
sample_period: US data from 1926; end date not verified here.
methodology: Uniform construction (tercile spreads with non-microcap breakpoints, capped value weights, one-month holding, four-month accounting lag); CAPM alphas; hierarchical Bayesian model with shrinkage and multiple-testing control; out-of-sample time-series and cross-country tests.
reported_effect: US replication rate (significant CAPM alpha, Bayesian) 82.4% vs the 35% reported by HXZ; OLS raw-return baseline 55.6% (61.3% excluding factors insignificant in the originals); 75.6% with a Benjamini-Yekutieli correction; 79.8%-81.5% with publication-bias-robust priors.
transaction_costs: Not deducted (alphas are gross).
survivorship_treatment: Includes CRSP delisting returns; missing performance-related delisting returns set to -30% (Shumway 1997).
out_of_sample_evidence: Factors hold up out-of-sample over time and across countries; post-publication alphas are positive but attenuated, somewhat more than their model predicts.
known_criticisms: CAPM alpha favours defensive/low-beta factors; addresses statistical replicability, not net-of-cost tradability.
replication_status: Counter-evidence to HXZ (2020).
post_publication_decay: Some decay of the strongest factors, consistent with arbitrage or data mining.
relevance_notes: Supports that factor themes are real, but the lab's question is recent, net, liquid-stock performance, which JKP do not address; jkpfactors.com can benchmark 2016-2024 factor returns.

title: A Taxonomy of Anomalies and Their Trading Costs
authors: Robert Novy-Marx; Mihail Velikov
anomaly: Meta-study: after realistic trading costs, high-turnover anomalies are unprofitable while many low/mid-turnover ones survive with cost mitigation.
dataset: 23 anomalies from CRSP/Compustat; effective spreads from Hasbrouck (2009) Gibbs estimates. Copy: https://mysimon.rochester.edu/novy-marx/research/ToAatTC.pdf
methodology: Value-weighted NYSE-breakpoint decile long-short strategies grouped by turnover; net returns using stock-level effective-spread estimates; cost mitigation (buy/hold spreads, less frequent rebalancing); capacity estimates.
reported_effect: Monthly gross -> net: momentum 1.33% -> 0.68% (t=2.45); IVOL 0.63% -> 0.11% (t=0.37); PEAD(SUE) 0.72% -> 0.26% (t=1.60); PEAD(CAR3) 0.91% -> 0.34% (t=2.41); short-run reversals 0.37% -> -1.28% (t=-6.02); industry momentum 0.93% -> -0.29%; seasonality 0.84% -> -0.62%. Most anomalies with under 50% monthly turnover can be made net-significant; few with higher turnover can.
transaction_costs: Central; buy/hold spread rules cut turnover by about 41% and costs by about 42% on average.
survivorship_treatment: Stock returns adjusted for delisting where applicable.
known_criticisms: Daily-data effective-spread estimates approximate small-trade costs and omit price impact for large trades; large institutions may trade more cheaply (Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz, as cited by Medhat & Schmeling 2022).
replication_status: Extended by Chen & Velikov (2023).
relevance_notes: Use as the lab's cost reference: a monthly signal with about 90% turnover (e.g. reversal) needs more than 1% per month gross just to break even; prefer slower signals and buy/hold buffers.

title: Zeroing In on the Expected Returns of Anomalies
authors: Andrew Y. Chen; Mihail Velikov
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 58(3), 968-1004
anomaly: Meta-study: after effective spreads, post-publication decay and the post-2000s trading-technology era, the average anomaly's expected net return is close to zero.
dataset: Long-short portfolios on published stock anomalies (120 in the May-2020 Fed working paper, https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/zeroing-in-on-the-expected-returns-of-anomalies.htm; a larger set in the published version).
methodology: Combine effective bid-ask spread costs, post-publication effects and a modern-era (early 2000s onward) subsample, with out-of-sample and empirical-Bayes data-mining adjustments and cost-optimized portfolios.
reported_effect: Published: the average anomaly's net expected return is 4 bp per month; the strongest anomalies net at best 10 bp after data-mining controls; several combination methods net about 20 bp. Working paper (120 anomalies): 8 bp per month, strongest 10-20 bp.
transaction_costs: Central (effective spreads); price impact omitted, so estimates are if anything optimistic.
out_of_sample_evidence: Uses post-publication and post-2000s periods as the relevant out-of-sample evidence.
known_criticisms: Cost-model approximations; does not cover option-based or intraday strategies.
replication_status: Builds on Chen-Zimmermann data and Novy-Marx-Velikov costs.
post_publication_decay: Incorporated directly.
relevance_notes: The most sobering prior for the lab: in the modern era a typical published stock anomaly is worth a few bp per month net; require strong out-of-sample, net-of-cost evidence before paper-trading any of these.

title: Have capital market anomalies attenuated in the recent era of high liquidity and trading activity?
authors: Tarun Chordia; Avanidhar Subrahmanyam; Qing Tong
anomaly: Meta-study: most prominent US equity anomalies attenuated after decimalization as liquidity and arbitrage activity rose.
dataset: Prominent US equity anomalies; hedge-fund assets, short interest and aggregate turnover as arbitrage proxies.
sample_period: Pre- vs post-decimalization (2001) comparison; exact span not verified.
methodology: Compare anomaly returns before and after decimalization and relate attenuation to hedge-fund assets, short interest and turnover.
reported_effect: The majority of anomalies attenuated, and average returns of a portfolio strategy based on prominent anomalies approximately halved after decimalization (abstract).
out_of_sample_evidence: Itself time-series out-of-sample evidence of decay.
replication_status: Consistent with McLean-Pontiff (2016) and Martineau (2022).
post_publication_decay: Attenuation after 2001 linked to arbitrage activity.
relevance_notes: 2016-2024 lies entirely in the high-liquidity regime; apply at least a 50% haircut to pre-2001 anomaly magnitudes before any cost deduction.
